CDU TEK (Russian federal dispatch agency) lists Orenburg-Novopskov among Kazakhstan's currently-used international transit lines (article context: 2021 KMG transit data, published 2023); Neftegas.info (2023-04-20) describes an active repair program on the line with gas supply to consumers maintained throughout -- both describe present-tense, ongoing operation. Status is inferable from context per the usual convention.

Both sources (and Neftegas.info) describe it as a 'магистральный газопровод' (trunk/main gas pipeline) -- consistent with 'transmission', not gathering/feeder.

Exact match, two independent sources. Kazakhstan Today quotes KazTransGas's own press release verbatim: 'Казахстанский участок газопровода Оренбург - Новопсков был введен в эксплуатацию в 1975 году' (the Kazakh section was commissioned in 1975). Ukrainian Wikipedia's dedicated article independently states commissioning year 1975 for the same line (citing Gazprom). Note this is explicitly the KAZAKH section's commissioning year in the KazTransGas source; I found no source suggesting the Russian/Ukrainian legs opened in a materially different year, so treating StartYear1=1975 as applying to the whole system is reasonable.

CDU TEK (Russian federal fuel-energy dispatch office) states, per-line (not a system aggregate): 'Оренбург - Новопсков (российский природный газ; 14,6 млрд куб. м в год)' -- an EXACT match to GEM's 14.60 bcm/y. Kept at tier=medium rather than high because I have only one source stating this exact per-line figure explicitly; however it cross-validates well against Intergas Central Asia's own Q2-2021 internal capacity register, which gives a COMBINED Soyuz+Orenburg-Novopskov actual-capacity figure of 40,820 million m3/year (40.82 bcm/y) -- and the same cdu.ru source separately states Soyuz alone = 25.2 bcm/y, so 25.2+14.6=39.8 bcm/y, closely matching the Intergas combined total (design vs actual-utilization variance is expected). This is the same 'system total vs per-line' pattern flagged on the CAC family (P2291 etc.), but here it resolves IN GEM'S FAVOR -- 14.6 is a genuine per-line figure, not a system total misapplied to a single string.

Major international cross-border trunk line moving gas from producing countries to China -- transmission, not a gathering/feeder line. Both sources describe it as a large-diameter (1,067mm/42in) international trunk pipeline.

thepeoplesmap.net: Line A operational since 2009, construction 'former [Line A] beginning to operate in December 2009'. AidData #54489: 'Line A achieved "state acceptance" on December 4, 2009' -- exact-month agreement across two independent sources.

Neither source states '15 bcm' for Line A in isolation; both state the COMBINED design capacity of Lines A+B and back out to 15 each. thepeoplesmap.net: 'The first two lines are designed to transport 30 bcm per year.' AidData #39997: 'Line A, B, and C provide 55 billion cubic meters (bcm) of gas to China per annum' and 'Line C has a designed capacity of 25 billion cubic meters per annum' -> A+B = 30 bcm combined. Every source surveyed treats Lines A and B as an identical symmetric twin-line design (same 1,067mm diameter, same length, built together 2008-2010), so an even 15/15 split is the universal characterization in the literature -- no source contradicts it. Confirmed at high tier on that basis.

Wikipedia infobox: 'Length 1,833 km (1,139 mi)'. Lowy Institute/The Interpreter: 'the 1,833-kilometre Central Asia-China Gas Pipeline'. A third source, thepeoplesmap.net, gives 1,837 km for the same corridor -- treated as ordinary cross-source rounding (<0.25% variance), not a conflict. This is the full Turkmenistan(Gedaim)-to-China(Horgos) length of one string, matching GEM's own recorded endpoints for this row (see validity note on scope).

Wikipedia infobox: 'Diameter 1,067 mm (42 in)'. offshore-technology.com independently states the same 1,067mm figure for Lines A/B, but is a likely shared upstream source with Wikipedia's own citation list (Wikipedia cites the same hydrocarbons-technology/offshore-technology profile for other facts on this page), so not counted as a second fully-independent origin -- tier held at medium rather than high. 42in=1,067mm is correct for Lines A/B specifically (Line C/P1124 is the larger 1,219mm/48in string) -- consistent with the orchestrator's prior finding that this is not a units error.

url_verifier's own docstring flags that its extractor does not reach the full text of large PDFs (this OIES working paper NG-155 is ~3.3MB); the automated content check FAILed on the exact tokens even though they are present. Manually downloaded and ran `pdftotext -layout`, confirming all three names verbatim: line 456-457 'the Chinese route was presumably supplied from Dauletabad, Turkmenistan's second largest field'; line 454 'the Galkynysh field has become the main source of exports to China'; line 425 'agreement (PSA) at Bagtyarlyk, output from which is exported to China' (OIES spells it 'Bagtyarlyk'; GEM's 'Bagtyyarlyk' is the same PSA block, common transliteration variant). One strong academic source naming all three -- tier medium per the 1-strong-source rule; a second source (thediplomat.com, 2026 article on Galkynysh) independently corroborates the Galkynysh-to-China link but does not name Dauletabad/Bagtyyarlyk, so it only partially corroborates. [QC] dropped unverified ref(s).

Line B (Kazakhstan Section) 'started operations in 2010' per offshore-technology.com's dedicated marketdata entry; Wikipedia corroborates 'the second line was completed by the end of 2010' and describes both lines as in service today (2022 EIA/Xinhua throughput data cited on the wiki page confirm ongoing operation). Two independent origins, both content-verified.
Both sources describe this uniformly as a natural gas pipeline carrying gas from Turkmen/Uzbek fields to China; not in dispute.
Described consistently across sources as a major cross-border trunk export system (Turkmenistan through Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to China), i.e. transmission, not a gathering/process line.

offshore-technology.com's Kazakhstan-section-specific page: Line B 'started operations in 2010' (elsewhere dated to 18 Oct 2010 state-acceptance). Wikipedia independently: 'the second line was completed by the end of 2010'. Not filling StartMonth1 (October) since no source gave an exact day/month I could independently corroborate to 2 sources — left blank rather than force it.

No source gives Line B's capacity in isolation; both cited sources give the combined Line A + Line B design capacity as 30 bcm/y (AidData #54489: 'transmit 30 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually' once all A+B compressor stations were operational by Oct 20 2012; offshore-technology.com: overall 'Capacity: 30 bcm/a'). Since Lines A and B are built as identical twin parallel pipes (same length, same diameter, same era) the even 15+15 split matches every source describing them as equal parallel lines; a third source (China AidData #91917, Uzbek section) independently states the same 30 bcm/a combined figure was reached by end 2011. Tier kept at 'high' on the combined figure; the even-split inference to 15.00 for this specific row is reasonable but not itself independently stated anywhere, so flagging that nuance rather than treating 15.00 as directly sourced.

offshore-technology.com states Line B length explicitly as '1,833 km' (same as Line A). Wikipedia: 'The length of Lines A, B, and C is about 1,833 kilometres'. This is the full Gedaim (Turkmenistan/Uzbekistan border) to Horgos (China) route length, consistent with GEM's own StartLocation/EndLocation for this row (Getaim→Horgos) — i.e. this row tracks the whole multi-country line, so the length is correctly the whole-route figure, not a Kazakhstan-only segment length. (The Kazakh segment alone is ~1,300–1,305 km per AidData #54489 and offshore-technology.com's marketdata page — consistent breakdown, not a conflict.)

offshore-technology.com's Kazakhstan-section page: 'maximum diameter of 42 inches'. Wikipedia: 'The diameter of each pipeline is 1,067 millimetres (42.0 in)'. 42in = 1,066.8mm ≈ 1,067mm, so DiameterUnits='in' is correct as-is (not a units error).

Bagtyyarlyk is firmly confirmed as the pipeline's origin field (Wikipedia: 'starts in Saman-Depe carrying natural gas from the Bagtyyarlyk gas fields'; Jamestown: 'newly opened Turkmen fields (Bagtyarlik, dedicated to China)'). Dauletabad is corroborated by Jamestown as feeding this export route (though it notes the field 'had until now been dedicated to exports northward to Russia', i.e. a relatively recent redirection). OSM/geometry (Tier 3, location-only): the OSM reconciliation run found an unnamed 614.7 km trace along this row's own drawn route corridor (disposition FRAGMENT_OF_EXISTING, route IoU 0.246 against GEM's already-'high'-accuracy route) -- independent satellite-derived geometry sits on top of the claimed corridor, consistent with existence. CLASSIFICATION: correct. Every source treats this as a 'магистральный газопровод' (trunk/transmission gas pipeline), never a gathering or feeder line -- Fuel=Gas and PipelineType=transmission are both well supported. DUPLICATE: checked against the roster's other 'Bukhara-Ural' row, P5695 (2,382 km, Gazli->Sverdlovsk Oblast, same Capacity=21.0, same Diameter='1000, 1020'). This is NOT a bibliographic duplicate/double-count -- Bukhara-Ural genuinely was built and is operated as TWO PARALLEL PHYSICAL STRINGS. The Giprospetsgaz institute's own account and multiple press pieces describe construction reaching Chelyabinsk first, then continuing on to Sverdlovsk/Nizhny Tagil -- i.e. an extension pattern consistent with GEM's two rows having different Russian-oblast endpoints (Chelyabinsk vs Sverdlovsk) off the same Gazli origin. BSE's 'первая очередь = 2,200 km' is an EXACT match for THIS row (P2289); summing P2289 (2,200) + P5695 (2,382) = 4,582 km, which sits within ~1-2% of the three independent whole-system totals found (BSE 4,503 km; Giprospetsgaz 4,464 km 'в однониточном исполнении'; uglevodorody.ru 4,537 km) -- strong circumstantial confirmation that P2289 and P5695 are the system's two real, distinct strings, not one pipe recorded twice. No merge recommended. Note for the record: intergas.kz's operating-division list (UMG Aktobe carries 'МГ «Бухара-Урал»' while UMG Kostanai separately also carries 'МГ «Бухара-Урал»') is consistent with, though does not on its own prove, a two-string reading.

resolutions.recommendation: Capacity=21.00 bcm/y is very likely the two-line SYSTEM's combined/design-era total, mis-stamped identically onto BOTH per-string rows (P2289 AND P5695 both carry 21.0) -- the same 'one system number on multiple strings' defect pattern flagged elsewhere in this pass. Do not treat as resolved; needs a genuine per-string figure or an explicit note that both rows intentionally share the system total. Separately, StartYear1=1963 is not cleanly corroborated -- the most authoritative source found (the pipeline's own design institute) points to gas reaching Chelyabinsk in 1964 and full two-line system commissioning in 1966, not 1963. Recommend re-checking against a source that states 1963 verbatim for the Gazli-Chelyabinsk leg specifically before treating it as confirmed.
resolutions.researcher_notes: CAPACITY (GEM: 21.00 bcm/y, identical on both P2289 and P5695): the number 21 IS independently attested, but every source that gives it frames it as the TWO-LINE SYSTEM total, never a single string's own throughput. The Great Soviet Encyclopedia entry (booksite.ru) states explicitly: 'двухниточная система Бухара — Урал ... пропускной способностью 21 млрд. м3 в год' -- 21 bcm/y for the whole two-line system as originally designed, immediately followed in the same sentence by the SAME source giving the Central Asia-Center two-line system's capacity as 25 bcm/y (a different pipeline family that shows the identical per-system-not-per-string framing). If GEM's two rows are each individually carrying the system's 21 bcm/y figure, the implied combined total (42 bcm/y) is roughly double any other figure found: the RPI 2009 industry report ('Oil and Gas Industry of Turkmenistan', s3.amazonaws.com/rgi-documents PDF -- note: fails url_verifier's automated content screen because the PDF is 3+ MB, a documented large-PDF false-negative; manually confirmed via `pdftotext -layout`, 'Bukhara-Urals'/'Bukhara-Ural' appear on lines 2172/3234/3243/3315) states the Bukhara-Ural TWO-LINE system's DESIGN capacity is 15 bcm/y, with actual current throughput only 3.5 bcm/y (Uzbek section) to 7.5 bcm/y (Russian section). KMG's own Annual Report table (ar2019.kmg.kz / ar2020.kmg.kz, EN PDFs -- same large-PDF false-negative on the automated screen, manually confirmed via pdftotext: 'Bukhara-Ural 2,382 44.6' [sic, actually 31.5 per the layout-preserved column] at line ~137/93) lists 'Bukhara-Ural' as a single table row at 2,382 km / 31.5 bcm/y -- notably, that LENGTH is an exact match for P5695, not P2289, yet KMG presents it as ONE row, reinforcing that KMG's own accounting does not cleanly split the system into two per-string figures either. Most tellingly, TWO independent 2023 sources describing the pipeline's actual current operation put the real combined throughput far lower still: ru.wikipedia.org states 'Пропускная мощность - 8 млрд. куб. м газа в год' (8 bcm/y) and gazeta.uz quotes an industry source giving the same figure ('«Бухара — Урал» — около 8 млрд кубометров'). So across five independent reference points the SYSTEM-level capacity ranges from 8 (current actual, 2023) to 15 (design, 2009) to 21 (design, Soviet-era BSE) to 31.5/44.6 (KMG AR2019-21, two different vintages of the same publisher, so really one origin) -- and NONE of them supports 21.0 bcm/y as this ONE STRING's own throughput. Recommend leaving Capacity unresolved/flagged rather than treating the existing 21.00 value as sourced. STARTYEAR1 (GEM: 1963): could not independently confirm. Giprospetsgaz's own institutional history (the design institute, arguably the single most authoritative source available) quotes a contemporaneous Chelyabinskiy Rabochiy newspaper article from NOVEMBER 1964 describing the first-stage construction as having just 'Дошли до Челябинска и двинулись к Свердловску' (reached Chelyabinsk and moved on toward Sverdlovsk) -- i.e. as of Nov 1964 the line was only just reaching Chelyabinsk, not already operating there since 1963. The same source states the pipeline (both lines together) was formally 'сдан в эксплуатацию' (commissioned) in 1966. Separately, Sverdlovsk (the endpoint of the OTHER string, P5695) got its first gas 1 December 1964 per both agenda-u.org and a search-summarized Yekaterinburg city-portal piece (ekburg.ru, page fetch failed/unreachable from this environment so not independently re-verified) -- and Chelyabinsk demonstrably received gas BEFORE that Dec-1964 Sverdlovsk date (agenda-u.org: '...Челябинским трубопрокатным заводами в 1964 году голубой факел запылал в Свердловске...' -- Chelyabinsk plants named as having already been supplied by the time Sverdlovsk lit up in 1964). Putting these together, the best-supported reading is that Chelyabinsk received first gas sometime in 1964 (not 1963), with full two-line system completion in 1966. This is only a one-year gap from GEM's 1963, and I did find one general-purpose web search summary asserting 'Первая нитка ... Газли-Челябинск ... запущена в 1963 году' -- but I could not trace that claim to a specific page I directly fetched and verified, so I am not citing it as a ref (standing rule 2: no fabricated/unverified sourcing). Net: StartYear1=1963 is plausible and only mildly in tension with the evidence, but not cleanly confirmed by the strongest available primary account.

resolutions.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: confirmed. CAC-2 ('вторая нитка', the second parallel line of the Soviet-era Central Asia-Center (CAC/SAC) transcontinental system) is a real, well-documented pipeline. Gazprom Transgaz Saratov's own corporate history (the sheet's own most-cited existing wiki source, backlinks=7) states explicitly: '1 октября 1970 года — введена в строй вторая нитка газопровода «Средняя Азия — Центр»' (second line commissioned Oct 1 1970) -- this EXACTLY matches GEM's StartYear1=1970. The live corporate site (saratov-tr.gazprom.ru) is unreachable from this environment (connection timeout, not a 404/410), so I verified via a Wayback Machine snapshot instead, which passed url_verifier (HTTP 200 + '1970'/'3600' present). CLASSIFICATION: transmission/Gas is correct -- this is unambiguously a Soviet-built transcontinental trunk gas pipeline, corroborated by multiple sources describing it as 'магистральный газопровод' / trunk line carrying Uzbek/Turkmen gas to Russia. DUPLICATE: checked against the Kazakhstan-gas roster's other two 'Central Asia–Center' rows, P5770 (len 3700, dia 1015/1220/1420) and P5771 (len blank, same diameter set). Per Gazprom Saratov's own history, the CAC system has (at least) FOUR distinct parallel lines: 1st stage/line 1967 (main trunk Kungrad→Voskresensk = 2,062 km, no diameter stated), 2nd line 1970 (no length/diameter stated in the source), 3rd line 1975 (3,600 km, 1220mm), 4th line 1976 (3,700 km, 1220+1420mm). P5770's length (3,700 km) is an EXACT match for the documented 4th line; P5771's diameter set matches P5770 and may be a related/aggregate entry. So P2291/P5770/P5771 most likely represent genuinely distinct PARALLEL PHYSICAL PIPES (not a bibliographic duplicate) -- this is the same legitimate pattern as Bukhara-Ural's two parallel strings. No merge recommended. However, see the separate SPEC finding below: the fact that all three rows carry the IDENTICAL Capacity=60.2 bcm/y is a genuine data-quality caveat, addressed in its own validity entry.

resolutions.recommendation: Revisit Owner1='Gazprom PJSC' at 100%. Two independent Russian sources say the Kazakh (and Uzbek) SAC segments belong to those countries, with Gazprom's role limited to a transportation/dispatcher contract -- 100% Gazprom ownership of a route GEM itself scopes as Turkmenistan→Russia (crossing Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan) is likely overstated. resolutions.researcher_notes: Two independent, verified sources contradict Owner1=Gazprom PJSC 100%: (1) Samruk-Kazyna (sk.kz) press release 'Информация по сотрудничеству с ОАО «Газпром»' (2011): describes SAC as 'the shortest international transit route for delivering Turkmen and Uzbek gas through Kazakhstan's territory' and states a 2011-2015 CONTRACT (not ownership transfer) governed gas transport through Kazakhstan between Gazprom and AO 'Intergas Central Asia' (ица), with a separate dispatcher agreement for managing/controlling the gas transport systems. (2) Interfax (2009), reporting on a 2009-04-09 pipeline rupture near the Turkmen/Uzbek border: 'Between Russian and Turkmen pipeline sections lie sections of the SAC system belonging to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan' -- explicit language of national ownership of the transiting segments, with Russia only taking custody of the gas at the Aleksandrov Gai compressor station on the border. Neither source supports Gazprom owning the Kazakh (or Uzbek) legs. If GEM's P2291 row is meant to model the pipe as it physically runs (Turkmenistan→Uzbekistan→Kazakhstan→Russia), a single 100%-Gazprom owner is not well supported by independent sourcing; Gazprom's documented role in Kazakhstan is contractual (transportation/dispatch), not proprietary.

CAPACITY (GEM: 60.20 bcm/y): this figure IS independently attested, but only as a WHOLE-SYSTEM / whole-corridor aggregate, never as a single-string figure. A peer-reviewed academic PDF (Neft i Gaz journal, Almaty, March 2019, by two named academics) states: '«Средняя Азия–Центр» в направлении Узбекистан–Казахстан–Россия: ... с пропускной способностью – 60,2 млрд м3/год, протяженностью – 3 962 км (оператор АО «Интергаз Центральная Азия»)' -- i.e. 60.2 bcm/y is stated for the WHOLE Uzbekistan–Kazakhstan–Russia transit corridor at 3,962 km, not for a single 1970-vintage 1220mm line. (Note: url_verifier FAILs the content check on this PDF -- 881KB/16pp, large-PDF extractor miss per the verifier's own documented false-negative class -- but I manually confirmed the exact text via `pdftotext -layout`; HTTP 200 is real and the content is present.) Separately, Interfax (2009) gives yet a THIRD aggregate figure -- 57 bcm/y design capacity, degraded to 52-53 bcm/y actual throughput due to pipe age -- for what it also treats as the whole SAC system. Three different aggregate-capacity figures (57 / 60.2 / and mingas.ru's later 80 bcm/y post-1985 buildout) from three sources, and GEM stamps 60.2 identically onto THREE separate string-level rows (P2291, P5770, P5771). This is the 'one system total on multiple strings' shape flagged by the orchestrator (India/HVJ-style defect) -- 60.2 bcm/y is a real, sourced number, but not evidence that CAC-2 alone carries 60.2 bcm/y of throughput.

resolutions.researcher_notes: The row is internally self-contradictory: StartState/Province='Mangystau' is a real Kazakhstan region, yet StartCountryOrArea='Turkmenistan'. Beyneu (the stated StartLocation) is a town in Mangystau Region, Kazakhstan — confirmed by two independent, non-GEM sources describing this exact pipeline (karakalpak-karakalpakstan.blogspot.com 2017 post 'Central Asia–Center gas pipeline system': western branch 'runs north...via Uzen in Kazakhstan to the Beyneu compressor station, where it meets the eastern branch'; ru.wikipedia.org 'Gazopipeline Central Asia-Center' article: western branch 'begins at Okarem near the Turkmen-Iran border...terminates at the Beyneu compressor station in Kazakhstan'). Both independent sources describe CAC-3 (the western branch) as ENDING at Beyneu, where it merges into the shared/eastern-branch corridor — neither mentions any continuation onward to a place called 'Gubkin' or to 'Belgorod Oblast'. I separately searched for the documented Russia-side terminus of the CAC system: both the karakalpak blog ('To Alexandrov Gay, Border of Kazakhstan/Russian Federation... From there two lines run northwest to Moscow, and two others proceed...to the North Caucasus-Moscow transmission system') and ru.wikipedia's article on Alexandrov Gay ('the settlement's largest industrial enterprise is a compressor station of the "Central Asia-Center" gas pipeline, Europe's largest') independently corroborate Alexandrov Gay / Petrovsk (Saratov Oblast) as the real KZ/Russia handover point for this system, continuing toward Moscow Oblast (which is consistent with sibling row P2291's EndState/Province='Moscow Oblast'). Belgorod Oblast is geographically far off that corridor (near the Ukraine border, well southwest of Saratov Oblast) and appears in none of the independent sources reviewed. This strongly suggests EndLocation='Gubkin'/EndState-Province='Belogorodsk Oblast' on this row is either a GEM-only construct (traceable only to gem.wiki, which per standing rule cannot be cited and should not be treated as corroboration) or a genuine locational error — possibly confusion with an unrelated regional gas-distribution line near Gubkin (a real Belgorod Oblast town with its own industrial gas infrastructure, unconnected to the Central Asian gas fields). Flagging rather than silently correcting, since I could not positively identify what the correct endpoint should be from independent sources alone.

resolutions.researcher_notes:
EXISTENCE/CLASSIFICATION: real, operating international trunk transmission pipeline. Independently confirmed by Wikipedia, The People's Map of Global China (thepeoplesmap.net, an independent research project, not GEM-derived), AidData (William & Mary's China-development-finance tracker, an academic/independent source, project #54489 'Kazakh Section of Lines A and B'), Lowy Institute/The Interpreter, and Oxford Institute for Energy Studies (OIES) working paper NG-155. All describe a real, built, operating gas trunk line (not gathering/feeder) moving Turkmen/Uzbek/Kazakh gas to China -- correctly classified transmission. Line A specifically achieved 'state acceptance' 4 Dec 2009 per AidData and began operating December 2009 per thepeoplesmap -- matches GEM StartYear1=2009 to the month.
DUPLICATE CHECK (the orchestrator's flagged question): P1124 (Line C), P2299 (Line A) and P2300 (Line B) are NOT duplicates/double-counts. They are three genuinely distinct, separately built and separately financed physical pipe strings run in the same corridor -- confirmed by AidData tracking three SEPARATE syndicated loans for the Kazakh sections of 'Lines A and B' (#54489) vs 'Line C' (#39997), and by Line C's different diameter/capacity (1,219mm/25 bcm vs 1,067mm/15 bcm each for A and B) being consistently reported everywhere. The shared LengthKnown=1833 on P1124/P2299/P2300 is legitimate, not an error: multiple independent sources (Wikipedia infobox 'Length 1,833 km'; Lowy Institute 'the 1,833-kilometre Central Asia-China Gas Pipeline'; thepeoplesmap.net 'The 1,837-kilometre-long pipelines'; a third-party technical summary reporting 'Line A and Line B, each measuring 1,833 km in length') all independently state that EACH parallel line (A, B, and by extension C, which runs the same corridor with a short additional Uzbek loop) is itself ~1,833-1,837 km end-to-end, because the three strings are laid in the same trench/corridor from Gedaim/Getaim (Turkmenistan) to Horgos (China). Minor variance (1833 vs 1837, <0.25%) is ordinary rounding across sources, not a data error.
SCOPE CAVEAT worth flagging for Baird's awareness (not a fix): GEM's LengthKnown=1833 is the FULL Turkmenistan-to-China length, consistent with the row's own recorded endpoints (StartLocation=Getaim/Turkmenistan, EndLocation=Horgos/Xinjiang/China) -- so it is internally consistent, not a defect. But the Kazakh-only portion of that same string is much shorter: AidData states the Kazakh sections of Lines A/B and of Line C each measure exactly 1,300 km ('These sections both measure 1300 km in length ... in Southern Kazakhstan from Shymkent to the Alataw Pass'), which matches Order 350 para 44's 'up to 1,300 km' Kazakh-portion figure already known to the sweep. No change recommended since GEM's own endpoints already declare the full multi-country route.

resolutions.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: unambiguously real and well documented across multiple independent origins — Wikipedia, offshore-technology.com (formerly hydrocarbons-technology.com; both a general project page and a page specifically for 'Central Asia–China Line B (Kazakhstan Section)'), the Lowy Institute, and two AidData (William & Mary) project records built from the underlying syndicated-loan documentation. CLASSIFICATION: correctly 'transmission' — this is the major Turkmenistan–Uzbekistan–Kazakhstan–China trunk export system, not a gathering/feeder line. DUPLICATE (the roster's structural flag): checked directly and REFUTED for this row. P2300 (Line B) is NOT the same physical pipe as P2299 (Line A) or P1124 (Line C) — it is a genuinely separate, separately-built, separately-commissioned parallel pipeline. offshore-technology.com's project page lists Line A (completed Dec 2009) and Line B (operational Oct 2010) as two distinct pipes that happen to share the identical 1,833 km route length and 1,067mm/42in diameter because they run side-by-side on the same corridor — the repeated '1,833.00 km' across P2299/P2300 in the roster is the CORRECT shared value, not a copy-paste error. This is independently corroborated at finer grain by AidData project #54489 (built from the CDB/China-financed loan documents for the Kazakh section): 'Lines A and B each measure 1300 km in length' running parallel 'from Shymkent to the Alataw Pass' in southern Kazakhstan, with combined Line A+Line B capacity of 30 bcm/y reached by Oct 20, 2012 — exactly matching GEM's 15.00 bcm/y x 2 (P2299+P2300) split. Line C (P1124) is a later, separately-negotiated third line (CNPC-Uzbekneftegaz agreement Sept 2011, ~2014 completion, 25 bcm/y) — confirmed as a distinct physical asset, not a duplicate of P2300. One out-of-scope note for a future P1124 check: Wikipedia states the diameter of 'each' of Lines A, B and C is 1,067mm/42in, which would conflict with GEM's own P1124 diameter of 1,219mm — flagging for the record since the roster raised it, but it is not this row's defect. FUEL SOURCE caveat: Wikipedia attributes the Galkynysh field specifically to Line D's supply (via Kyrgyzstan/Tajikistan) and names Bagtyyarlyk (at Saman-Depe) plus Iolotan/Sag Kenar as the Lines A/B/C source fields; Jamestown's 2010 analysis separately ties both Dauletabad and Bagtyarlik to the China-bound export system (noting Dauletabad 'had until now been dedicated to exports northward to Russia', i.e. only recently redirected to this pipeline). GEM's three-field FuelSource list for P2300 is plausible and broadly corroborated but not confirmed by one single authoritative per-line source — treat as medium confidence, not a concern. OPERATOR caveat: GEM lists 'Turkmengaz, Uztransgaz, Intergas Central Asia'. Intergas Central Asia's own site confirms it operates Kazakhstan's main gas pipeline system generally, but two independent AidData project pages (built from the actual JV/loan documents) identify the entity specifically chartered to construct, finance AND operate the Kazakh section of this pipeline as 'Asian Gas Pipeline LLP' (AGP), a 50/50 JV of KazTransGas and CNPC (via its subsidiary Trans-Asia Gas Pipeline Co. Ltd) — not Intergas Central Asia by name. This may just be a level-of-detail gap (AGP as legal JV vs. Intergas as the domestic O&M arm under an operating agreement) rather than an error, so flagged as a caveat for Update rather than a hard concern.

This also fits the wider network logic checked against 2 independent secondary sources (en.wikipedia.org CAC infobox + karakalpak-karakalpakstan.blogspot.com, both describing the whole CAC system's 'western branch'/CAC-3 running from Okarem, Turkmenistan north through Beyneu to Alexandrov Gay, Russia, ~2,000 km total): Beyneu is a mid-route junction, not an endpoint of a ~1,000 km stand-alone segment — gas arriving at Beyneu from Turkmenistan splits further, part continuing NORTH toward Russia (the P2291/P2292/P5770/P5771 'Central Asia-Center' family) and part heading SOUTH to Zhanaozen/Aktau for local Mangystau supply (P5772 'Beyneu-Zhanaozen' + the P3948 Zhanaozen-Zhetybai-Aktau family) — consistent with dknews.kz explicitly calling Zhanaozen-Zhetybai-Aktau 'a continuation of' Okarem-Beyneu. I could not find a second numeric-length source pinpointing exactly 309.8/233 km (verifier's automated content-check fails on this specific PDF for every ASCII token tried — '309,8', '1972-1974', '1972', even 'Интергаз' — despite a clean HTTP 200; this matches the documented url_verifier caveat that a content FAIL on a PDF proves nothing, and I confirmed the text is genuinely present via `pdftotext -layout` locally: the extracted row reads verbatim 'Окарем-Бейнеу 1200 309,8 1972-1974 8 260 3 100 88%'), so I'm treating the length correction as high-confidence on a single strong primary/operator source rather than double-independently-numerically-confirmed. Recommend Update apply the correction and note the untracked loop line to the redundancy-cluster/discovery leg.

That URL is genuinely DEAD today (confirmed HTTP 404 via direct curl, not a TLS artifact), but I recovered it via a Wayback Machine snapshot (2024-01-13) and read the actual table (verified by rendering the PDF page to an image, not just pdftotext, to rule out OCR error): 'Zhanazhol-Oktyabrsk-Aktobe [4] | 1988 | 270/1 line | 0.9/520' -- i.e. the source itself says diameter 520 mm, not GEM's 530 (a small, likely-typo-level 1.9% gap). That table's own footnote [4] traces to an unlabeled ~2010-2013 'Concept of Gas Transport System Development' PowerPoint of unclear authorship/provenance, and the paper's own concluding sentence explicitly warns: 'the presented analysis shows that numerical data on the characteristics of Kazakhstan's gas pipelines are CONTRADICTORY and require systematization' -- i.e. even this source doesn't claim to be authoritative. Against that single, self-admittedly-shaky compilation, TWO independent, more current, mutually-reinforcing sources disagree: (1) АО «Интергаз Центральная Азия»'s OWN 2015 annual report, filed with the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (kase.kz/files/emitters/INCA/incap_2015_rus.pdf, live, 128pp; verified by downloading and reading with pdftotext -layout plus a rendered-page screenshot of the actual system table) -- this is the ACTUAL PIPELINE OPERATOR's own audited filing, not a secondary compilation -- lists a line it calls (without 'Oktyabrsk') 'Zhanazhol-Aktobe', commissioned 2005, length 143 km, design capacity 0.697 bln m3/yr, 2015 actual throughput 0.667 bln m3 (95.7% utilization); (2) the registry's own GulfPub crosswalk (Tier 2, PE World Map, scraped from QazaqGaz's current corporate 'General information' page, qazaqgaz.kz/en/obshchaya-informaciya) independently returns TWO segments both named exactly 'Zhanazhol - Aktobe', totaling 102.998 + 51.499 = 154.5 km -- in the same ~143-155 km neighborhood as the 2015 filing, not GEM's 270. (GulfPub's route geometry for both segments has poor overlap with GEM's own drawn route, IoU 0.03 and 0.21, so even geometrically these may not trace the identical corridor GEM has mapped.) Capacity is the one field NOT in dispute: GEM's live sheet value (0.70 bcm/y) is well supported -- it matches the 2015 Intergaz filing's 0.697 almost exactly, and independently matches Forbes 2022's stated design figure of 80,000 m3/hour (=0.7008 bcm/yr at 8760 h/yr) -- TWO independent sources agreeing closely, high tier. (gem.wiki's own infobox still carries the STALE 0.9 bcm/y figure from the single 2013 compilation, which the sheet has already correctly moved away from -- no further action needed on Capacity.) My working theory, offered as a lead for Update rather than a settled finding: the 1988-vintage, 270 km, 520mm 'Zhanazhol-Oktyabrsk-Aktobe' line and the 2005-vintage, 143-155 km 'Zhanazhol-Aktobe' line reported by Intergaz TsA's own annual filing may be two different physical assets (an original Soviet-era line plus a shorter parallel/replacement string built in 2005), both still bundled under intergas.kz's current listing ('with loopings' = with parallel loop sections) -- in which case P3944 may be under-representing the corridor (one row where there should be two) rather than simply carrying a wrong number. I did not find any source resolving this cleanly, so I'm flagging it rather than picking a number myself.

GEM's Capacity=0.50 bcm/y (500 million m3/year) traces to 2007 pre-construction planning language: both the KazInform article and the Government Decree describe 'final/ultimate volumes up to 500 million cubic meters per year' as the DESIGN TARGET at the time the project was approved (with an initial ramp-up figure of only 120 million m3/y from the existing gas-treatment unit). However, Intergas Central Asia's own current capacity register — 'Информация о наличии существующей мощности Магистральных Газопроводов АО «Интергаз Центральная Азия», по состоянию на 01.01.2025' (intergas.kz PDF, verified by direct pdftotext/pdfplumber read, not just the url_verifier substring screen which false-negatived on the space-separated '2 520' token) — lists 'Карачаганак-Уральск: диаметр 508мм, протяженность 152км, год ввода 2011' with BOTH Проектная (design) and Фактическая на 2024 (actual-2024) capacity columns reading 2,520 million m3/year (28% utilization in 2024). I verified the column alignment against pdfplumber word x-coordinates row-by-row (matches the same x0 pattern as the neighboring Saryarka row, which is unambiguous in the plain-text extraction) — this is not a misread. A 508mm/20-inch pipe carrying only 500 mcm/y over 152km would be dramatically oversized hydraulically, whereas 2,520 mcm/y is a physically sensible throughput for that diameter — which further supports the 2024 register over the 2007 planning figure as the value that actually reflects what got built. Diameter (508mm) and length (152km, vs. sheet's 152.00) and StartYear1 (2011) all independently CONFIRM against this same register plus the ecoportal.kz filing (152.13km, 2011) — those three fields are fine. Only Capacity is off, and it's off by a lot. Note a secondary complication: a TMK (pipe manufacturer) press release from Dec 2009 about pipe delivered 'for construction of the Karachaganak-Uralsk gas pipeline' lists diameters of 273mm (bulk, 6,000t), 219mm (250t) and 1016mm (1,900t) — none of which is 508mm. Given the 2007 Decree's own text describes the same overall project as including separate high-pressure BRANCH pipelines to two villages (Novopavlovka, Zhympity) in addition to the 152km main line, I read the TMK figures as most likely covering that mixed scope (main line + branches + a large-diameter insert section) rather than being the single nominal diameter of the registered 152km trunk itself — so I did not treat 508mm as a concern, only Capacity.

resolutions.recommendation: Investigate whether P3948 ('Segment I', Uzen->Aktau, 149.10 km, 720mm, built 1974) is a legacy whole-route aggregate that double-counts the three granular segment rows P5776 (Kaz GPP-KS-Zhanaozen, 17.8 km, 720mm, built 1974) + P5777 (Zhanaozen-Zhetybay, 60.7 km, built 2008) + P5783 (Zhetybay-Aktau, 70.8 km, built 1968) -- those three sum to 149.30 km, within 0.20 km (0.13%) of P3948's own length, and P3948 exactly shares P5776's diameter (720mm) and start year (1974). If a human confirms P3948 is not an independently surveyed physical 'first string' distinct from the other rows, it should be merged/retired rather than left standing as a fourth, redundant whole-corridor entry -- do not delete unilaterally.
resolutions.researcher_notes: GEM's own roster shows five rows sharing this pipeline name: P3948 (Uzen->Aktau, 149.1 km, dia 720mm, cap 4.54, StartYear1 1974), P5776 (Kaz GPP->Uzen, 17.8 km, dia 720mm, cap 4.54, StartYear1 1974), P5777 (Uzen->Zhetybay, 60.7 km, dia 530mm, cap 4.54, StartYear1 2008), P5783 (Zhetybay->Aktau, 70.8 km, dia 529mm, cap 4.54, StartYear1 1968), and P5784 (Zhetybay->Kuryk branch, 70.0 km, cap 3.60 -- a separate spur, not part of this concern). 17.8+60.7+70.8 = 149.3 km, matching P3948's 149.10 km to within 0.13% -- far too precise to be a coincidental parallel-corridor match. P3948's diameter (720mm) and StartYear1 (1974) are identical to P5776's, not to P5777/P5783's (530/529mm, 2008/1968), which is the signature of a row that was built by copying one child segment's attributes and summing all children's lengths, rather than an independently surveyed pipe. Working against a clean 'duplicate, delete it' verdict: (1) P3948's own endpoints read Uzen->Aktau, which by GEM's own geography should exclude the Kaz GPP->Uzen leg (P5776) -- if P3948 really were the sum of all three, its endpoints should read Kaz GPP->Aktau, so the endpoint labeling is internally inconsistent with the apparent length-summing; (2) Intergas's own 2023 and 2024 annual reports (intergas.kz upload d8uwec4lky88goo8gks4.pdf, verified 200) explicitly describe a 2023 project 'Капитальный ремонт 3-х ниток МГ <<Жанаозен-Жетыбай-Актау>>' -- capital repair of THREE strings of the Zhanaozen-Zhetybay-Aktau trunk -- confirming the underlying trunk genuinely is a multi-string (3-string) system, so a distinct String I could legitimately exist in principle. The same annual report also lists 'МГ <<КазГПЗ-КС <<Жанаозен>>' (Kaz GPP-CS Zhanaozen) as a SEPARATELY NAMED pipeline from 'МГ <<Жанаозен-Жетыбай-Актау>>' in Intergas's own facility inventory under UMG Aktau -- i.e. Intergas itself does not treat the Kaz GPP-Zhanaozen leg (P5776) as 'Segment II' of the Zhanaozen-Zhetybay-Aktau system the way GEM's SegmentName field implies, which is a secondary attribution wrinkle worth a human look but not this row's primary problem. Net: the numeric match is too exact to ignore, but I could not find an independent source that names 'String I' specifically at 149.1 km, so I'm flagging this as a concern for human adjudication (merge candidate) rather than asserting it outright.

resolutions.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: strongly confirmed, independent of the sheet's own wiki citations. Kazinform (inform.kz, 2022) reports a scheduled Aug 1-25 2022 shutdown of the 'Kartaly-Rudny main gas pipeline' for corrosion repairs, calling it 'one of the first gas pipelines put into operation in Kazakhstan' and stating it has run continuously since 1965. Naша Газета/ng.kz (26 Jul 2024, quoting QazaqGaz deputy chairman Akbar Tulegenov at the Kostanay INVEST-2024 forum) states the pipeline 'Kartaly-Rudny' currently delivers the LARGEST share of gas reaching Kostanai region, is 1960s-built, single-line, and runs almost continuously -- and is the explicit reason QazaqGaz is building a $1B+ replacement line (CS-14 Bukhara-Ural, Aktobe -> Kostanai city, 630 km, 4.1 bcm/y, Qatari JV with Power International Holding/UCC Holding, 2023-2026) for energy-security diversification. A Kazakhstan government ecology public-hearing filing (hearings.ndbecology.gov.kz, doc 214986 -- a 2019-era reconstruction project for the pipeline's underwater crossing of the Karatomar reservoir at km 154-155) independently documents the same asset: 'Введен в эксплуатацию в 1965 г.' (commissioned 1965), serviced by Kostanai LPU, near the village Naberezhny, with cathodic-protection stations at km 151 and km 156. Intergas Central Asia's own 2015 KASE-filed annual report (kase.kz/files/emitters/INCA/incap_2015_rus.pdf) lists 'Карталы - Рудный' among UMG Kostanai's assets and, separately, 'Карталы-Рудный-Кустанай' in its system-inventory table at 1965/1,6 bcm-y design/0,461 bcm actual (28.8% utilization). This is a real, actively-monitored, currently-operating trunk line -- no existence concern. CLASSIFICATION: correctly a gas transmission trunk line (all sources call it 'магистральный газопровод'/main gas pipeline), not a gathering/feeder line -- confirmed. DUPLICATE: checked against the 39-pipeline Kazakhstan-gas roster; no other row shares this route or these endpoints (Kartaly/Chelyabinsk Oblast Russia -> Rudny -> Kostanai) -- unique, not a double-count. OWNERSHIP CHAIN: Intergas Central Asia's 2015 annual report traces its own share history (Intergas International B.V. -> KazTransGaz 2010 -> ultimately KazMunayGas/Samruk-Kazyna); intergas.kz's current 'About the company' page states in English: 'The Company is a subsidiary of the National Company QazaqGaz, JSC' -- confirms GEM's Owner1=QazaqGaz 100% is the CURRENT correct entity (QazaqGaz being the post-2021 successor once the gas transmission arm was carved out of KazMunayGas/KazTransGaz per this project's own country notes), and confirms Operator='AO Intergaz Tsentralnaya Aziya' is correct. Both intergas.kz pages I cite are the same origin as the operator's own self-report (medium tier alone), but the fact of Intergas as operator/QazaqGaz as parent is also implicit in ng.kz's independent framing of 'QazaqGaz' as the national operator responsible for this exact pipeline's replacement -- so tier medium-high overall on ownership.

resolutions.recommendation: Correct FuelSource. 'Karachaganak Oil and Gas Field, Ural' is almost certainly a copy-paste artifact from the roster's OTHER Kazakhstan pipeline sourced from Karachaganak (P3947 Karachaganak-Uralsk Gas Pipeline: Karachaganak -> West Kazakhstan). P3955's actual gas source, per an independent news source, is imported Russian gas, tapped off the Bukhara-Ural trunk system at the Kartaly compressor station -- not the Karachaganak field, which is ~1,000+ km away in West Kazakhstan and cannot plausibly feed a pipeline whose start point is in Chelyabinsk Oblast, Russia.
resolutions.researcher_notes: GEM FuelSource='Karachaganak Oil and Gas Field, Ural'. This is geographically implausible: P3955's own StartLocation/StartState-Province/StartCountryOrArea fields (Kartaly, Kartalinsky District, Chelyabinsk region, RUSSIA) place its source point in Russia, ~1,000+ km from the Karachaganak field in West Kazakhstan (which feeds the roster's SEPARATE P3947 Karachaganak-Uralsk Gas Pipeline, Karachaganak -> West Kazakhstan, cap 0.5 bcm/y) -- gas cannot flow from Karachaganak to Kartaly against/across the existing pipeline grid without an unrecorded, implausible detour. Independent confirmation of the true source: ng.kz (26 Jul 2024, on-record quote from QazaqGaz deputy chairman) states plainly of this exact pipeline, 'газ поступает российский' (the gas is Russian), citing this as the specific energy-security vulnerability motivating the new replacement pipeline. A separate open-web search independently corroborates the mechanism: 'КС Карталы' (Kartaly compressor station) is a linear station ON the Bukhara-Ural (Бухара-Урал) trunk pipeline, which transits Central Asian (Uzbek/Turkmen-origin) gas through Kazakhstan into Russia -- meaning Kartaly is the point where gas is tapped back OFF the Bukhara-Ural/Russian transit system into Kazakhstan via this branch line, consistent with 'Russian gas' framing even though its ultimate origin traces further back to Central Asia. Either way, 'Karachaganak Oil and Gas Field' is not a plausible fuel source for this line. I did not find a primary source naming the exact originating Russian field/system precisely enough to propose a specific replacement value (no fabrication per standing rule 2) -- recommending the cell be corrected to something in the family of 'Imported (Russian gas grid, via Bukhara-Ural system tapped at Kartaly)' pending a source that names it more precisely.

That report's 'TRUNK PIPELINE GAS TRANSPORTATION' table gives only ONE combined row: 'BGR-TBA, Gazli-Shymkent | 2,462 km | 10.2 bln m3/year' -- it does NOT break the two pipelines out individually. 877 km is exactly 2,462 minus 1,585 (GEM's own P0739 BGR-TBA length), i.e. an arithmetic residual/inferred split from the combined total, not an independently reported per-line figure -- the source cited for 'Length: 877 km' on gem.wiki does not actually state 877 km anywhere.
